sections.content: If you've been watching interest rates, home prices, and the evening news, you've probably asked yourself: is now a good time to invest in real estate? It's a fair question. Mortgage rates hovered near 7% through much of 2024 and into 2025, and median home prices in many metros are still well above pre-pandemic levels. But here's what experienced investors already know — the best time to invest is rarely obvious. The people who built wealth in real estate didn't wait for perfect conditions. They learned to find opportunity inside the chaos.
What the 2025 Real Estate Market Actually Looks Like

Let's start with the facts. As of early 2025, the national median home price sits around $410,000, up roughly 4% year-over-year. Inventory is slowly recovering from its historic lows, with active listings up about 20% compared to 2023 in many markets. At the same time, mortgage rates have come off their 2023 peaks but remain elevated, creating a market where motivated sellers are increasingly common — especially among homeowners who bought at the top and are now facing financial pressure.

For investors, this is actually a more favorable environment than the frenzied bidding wars of 2021. When competition cools and seller motivation rises, deal-finders have more room to negotiate. The key is knowing which markets to focus on and how to quickly evaluate whether a property pencils out as a profitable investment.
The Case For Investing Right Now
More Motivated Sellers Are Entering the Market

One of the clearest signals that now is a reasonable time to invest is the rise in distressed and motivated sellers. Pre-foreclosure filings have climbed steadily since the end of pandemic-era forbearance programs. In Q4 2024, ATTOM Data reported foreclosure activity at levels not seen since 2019. These sellers often need to move quickly and are more open to discounted offers — exactly the conditions wholesalers and fix-and-flip investors look for.
Rental Demand Remains Strong

High home prices and elevated mortgage rates have pushed more Americans into renting for longer. National vacancy rates for single-family rentals remain below 6%, and average rents have held firm in most major metros. If you're evaluating a buy-and-hold investment, the income side of the equation is still working in your favor. Sun Belt cities in particular continue to see strong in-migration, which supports rental occupancy and appreciation. Markets like [Atlanta](https://aiwholesail.com/markets/atlanta-ga), [Dallas](https://aiwholesail.com/markets/dallas-tx), and [Phoenix](https://aiwholesail.com/markets/phoenix-az) are consistently showing strong fundamentals for rental investors.

"The best time to buy real estate was 20 years ago. The second best time is now. What changes isn't the opportunity — it's your strategy." — A principle echoed by investors from Warren Buffett to Robert Kiyosaki
The Case For Caution: What to Watch Out For

Honest advice means addressing the real risks too. Higher borrowing costs directly impact your cash flow projections. A rental property that would have cashflowed $400 per month with a 3.5% loan might barely break even at 7%. This means your buy price matters more than ever. Overpaying in today's market leaves almost no margin for error if values soften or a major repair hits unexpectedly.

items: Run conservative numbers: Use current market rents, not optimistic projections, when calculating cash flow
Account for higher carrying costs: Insurance premiums and property taxes have risen sharply in many states
Don't bank on appreciation alone: Cash flow should justify the deal even without price growth
Watch your debt-service coverage ratio (DSCR): Many lenders now want a DSCR of at least 1.25 for investment loans
Verify your exit strategy: If flipping, confirm ARV against recent comps — not 2021 peak prices

Which Investment Strategies Work Best Right Now?
Wholesaling: Low Capital, High Opportunity

Wholesaling is one of the most accessible strategies in a high-rate environment because you're not taking on a mortgage. You find deeply discounted properties, put them under contract, and assign the contract to a cash buyer for a fee — typically $5,000 to $25,000 per deal. With more motivated sellers entering the market, deal flow for wholesalers is improving. If you're new to this strategy, our [Wholesaling Real Estate for Beginners guide](https://aiwholesail.com/guides/wholesaling-real-estate-for-beginners) walks you through the entire process step by step.
BRRRR: Buy Right and Refinance When Rates Drop

The BRRRR method (Buy, Rehab, Rent, Refinance, Repeat) is still viable if you buy at a significant discount and can carry the property through a renovation using cash or a short-term hard money loan. Investors using this strategy today are banking on refinancing into a lower rate in 12 to 24 months if the Federal Reserve continues to ease. The math only works if you buy well below market value — which is why deal-finding skills matter more right now than at any point in the last decade.
Subject-To and Creative Finance Deals

Creative financing strategies have surged in popularity as a direct response to high rates. A subject-to deal lets you take over the seller's existing mortgage — including their 3% or 4% interest rate from 2020 or 2021 — without qualifying for a new loan. Seller financing and lease options are also giving investors ways to structure deals that cash flow even in today's environment. These strategies require more negotiation skill but can unlock deals that don't work any other way.
Step-by-Step: How to Evaluate a Deal in Today's Market

items: Step 1 – Research the market: Focus on areas with job growth, population growth, and rising rents. Start with high-performing metros before exploring smaller markets
Step 2 – Find your ARV: Pull recent sold comps within 0.5 miles, same bedroom and bath count, sold within 90 days. Be conservative
Step 3 – Estimate repair costs: Get at least two contractor quotes or use $15–25 per square foot for light rehabs and $35–50 for full gut jobs
Step 4 – Apply the 70% rule (for flips): Maximum offer = (ARV × 70%) minus repair costs. This builds in your profit and holding costs
Step 5 – Run a cash flow analysis (for rentals): Subtract mortgage payment, taxes, insurance, vacancy (8%), and maintenance (10% of rent) from gross rent
Step 6 – Make your offer and negotiate: In today's market, lowball offers are more likely to get a response than they were in 2021 — submit them confidently

The Bottom Line: Timing vs. Strategy

So is now a good time to invest in real estate? The honest answer is: it depends on your strategy, your market, and your ability to find below-market deals. It is not a good time to overpay and hope for appreciation. It is a good time to find motivated sellers, negotiate aggressively, and build a portfolio of assets that produce income from day one. The investors who will look back at 2025 as a great buying window are the ones taking disciplined action right now — not waiting on the sidelines for rates to drop.
